title: The Gatha of Guru Arjan
hook: a short, dense poem in an old literary style (ang 1360)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sehskriti's warnings: katanch, where is mother, where is father. Your line was passing things.

A spoonful of honey and a glass of sugar water can hold the same sweetness. One you sip for a while. The other you taste all at once, and it stays on the tongue. On Ang thirteen hundred sixty of the Guru Granth Sahib sits a short composition by Guru Arjan called the Gatha. It's the honey: short, packed, written in an old literary style, every line carrying more than its size suggests. You don't read it quickly. You let it sit on the tongue.
screen: `HONEY AND SUGAR WATER.` → `ANG 1360.` → `LET IT SIT ON THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Gatha is often glossed as a verse or a song, and here it's the heading of the composition itself. It's short and dense, in an old literary style. Like the Sehskriti, its words carry an older, learned sound, so some Sikhs study it with someone who knows the vocabulary. Its opening lines, paraphrased: camphor, flowers and perfume, touching the human body, become soiled. That's a startling start. Most of us think of the body as the thing that needs perfume, and here the perfume is what gets dirty. Read on, and the Gatha keeps pointing past the body's surface: to the Name, the company of the holy, the Lord's praise. Each line works like a seed, small enough to hold in your palm, holding a whole tree. That's what dense means. Not difficult for its own sake, but folded, so it opens slowly. A long hymn can carry you along by its flow. A dense one asks you to stop: read a phrase, put it down, look at it from another side. A reader can come back to a single line for days. Some truths arrive in a flood of words. Others come in a spoonful, and the work is to let them dissolve.
screen: `GATHA: A VERSE, A SONG.` · `CAMPHOR AND FLOWERS, SOILED.` · `A SEED THAT HOLDS A TREE.` · `A DENSE LINE ASKS YOU TO STOP.` · then, large: `DENSE AND SHORT.`

segments.voice: If you can find the Gatha on Ang thirteen hundred sixty, read only its first line, in Gurmukhi or in translation; if not, take today's paraphrase: camphor and flowers, touching the body, become soiled. Close your eyes, let the line sit, and turn it over once to see what surprises you. One line, all the way down.
Gatha. A verse, a song; Guru Arjan's short, dense composition in an old literary style on Ang thirteen hundred sixty. Today's word.
Your line: dense and short. A small line can hold a whole tree. That's day twelve hundred five.

howItsDone: The Gatha of Guru Arjan is read as part of the Guru Granth Sahib's closing sections; because of its old literary vocabulary, some Sikhs study it with a giani or a teeka, line by line.
